days.label: Hoshana Rabbah
days.sublabel: 21 Tishri · the Day of the Willow

themes.title: Hoshanot and the Day of the Willow
themes.intro: Hoshanot, the litanies recited during Sukkot and above all at its end, are among the most common Sukkot texts in the Genizah. Writers of the 10th to the 13th century often call Hoshana Rabbah 'the Day of the Willow' (יום ערבה): the phrase appears in the al-ʿĀqūlī calendar (T-S K2.8), in the pocket booklet Halper 251, in a yeshiva letter of about 1045 (T-S NS 320.42) and in communal accounts of 1219 (T-S NS J221). Among the fragments are hoshanot by Eleazar ha-Kallir and several leaves that catalogues assign to the hoshanot of Saadya Gaon's Siddur, whose edition (Davidson, Assaf and Joel, 1941) was itself built from a Bodleian manuscript and Genizah fragments; how many separate copies of the Siddur these leaves represent has not been worked out. One of the oldest witnesses is on reused parchment: after a Palestinian marriage contract, likely of the 10th century, was discarded, a poet cut it and wrote on its back a hoshanot text for the end of Sukkot in seven alphabetic stanzas (T-S 24.68; Friedman, Jewish Marriage in Palestine II, no. 3).
hedges: Assignments to Saadya's Siddur come from catalogue entries (KTIV, catalogue notes); how many copies they represent is an open question.
We found no open-access modern study devoted to hoshanot in the Genizah; the standard edition of the Ashkenazi-rite texts is Goldschmidt and Fraenkel (1981).

themes.title: Festival prayers
themes.intro: The fixed prayers of the festival survive in many small pieces of prayer books. Catalogue entries name Musaf services for particular days (the sixth and seventh days on T-S AS 109.184 and T-S NS 120.64), a Kiddush for Sukkot, the Shema and its blessings for the festival, and Amidah texts for Sukkot and Shemini Atzeret in the Palestinian rite (T-S B13.16, T-S NS 120.64). The Palestinian rite, which the Genizah preserves alongside the Babylonian one, is the subject of Ezra Fleischer's standard study of its prayers and customs (1988). A Karaite prayer book (T-S NS 120.9) has Karaite prayers for the additional services of Shavuot, Rosh ha-Shanah and Sukkot. Most of these leaves have no transcription yet: the identification on each card is the catalogue's.
hedges: Identifications rest on the catalogue entries quoted on each card; most leaves are untranscribed.

themes.title: Poems for Sukkot
themes.intro: Much of the Genizah's Sukkot material is liturgical poetry written for the festival services: qedushtaot, shivʿatot, yotserot and maʿaravot. The poets named in the catalogue entries run from the classical Palestinian poets Yannai and Eleazar ha-Kallir (edited by Rabinovitz and studied by Elizur) to later figures such as Yosef ibn Avitur and Shemuel ha-Shelishi. Poems also travelled with their owners: the India trader Abraham Ben Yijū copied two poems by Judah ha-Levi on a piece of cloth, the first an ofan for Sukkot (T-S 16.31; Goitein and Friedman, India Traders, pp. 66-68), and on the back of an Aden court letter he copied a Maʿariv for Sukkot (NLI 4° 577.2/15; India Book II, no. 36). Where catalogues disagree about a poem's occasion, both readings are shown.
hedges: Attributions and occasions come from catalogue entries and have mostly not been checked against the text.
CAJS Genizah 259: the public title and most KTIV entries say Shavuot; one KTIV description says Tabernacles (needs a specialist).
Bodl. MS heb. e 39/94: catalogue cards say a yotser for Sukkot, another card a yotser for Shemini Atzeret.

contested.claim: Occasion of Bodl. MS heb. e 39/94

themes.title: Shemini Atzeret and the prayer for rain
themes.intro: The eighth day that closes the festival has its own prayers and poems, and the prayer for rain belongs to it, as the heading 'תפילת גשם לשמיני עצרת' on T-S H7.2 puts it. Shulamit Elizur's study of early shivʿatot for rain (Ginzei Qedem 1, 2005) is built on Genizah fragments, and a 2021 study notes that two Sephardic Genizah copies of Kallir's rain shivʿata 'Af beri' combine its first stanzas with a second composition. The catalogues also name qedushtaot and qerovot for the day by Yannai, by Pinhas and by Sahlan b. Avraham, whose poem survives in two witnesses. A new identification, reported by the Princeton Geniza Project, is striking: an Arabic deed of 874, which PGP calls the oldest Arabic document in the Genizah, was reused on its back for a Shemini Atzeret piyyut (T-S H7.45). That identification was made in August 2026 and PGP says it requires further study.
hedges: T-S H7.45 rests on one very recent source (PGP 42118, identified by Alan Elbaum, August 2026); PGP says it 'requires further study'.
In Genizah documents 'ʿAtzeret' on its own commonly means Shavuot; do not read it as Shemini Atzeret without a clear context.

themes.title: Simhat Torah and the reading cycle
themes.intro: In the Palestinian custom the Torah was read over a cycle of about three to three and a half years. Benjamin of Tudela (c. 1170) describes two synagogues in Fustat, the Palestinians finishing the Torah in three years, and the two congregations praying together on Simhat Torah and on Shavuot. The fullest Genizah witness is 'Seder Fustat A', prayer-book leaves of Fustat's Palestinian (Shami) congregation copied in the early 13th century by its cantor Yedutun ha-Levi (Fleischer; Rand; Shweka 2020): it orders the second festival day of Shemini Atzeret, on which the Babylonians' Simhat Torah was held in the Palestinians' synagogue. That the two congregations celebrated it jointly is Fleischer's and Shweka's inference, supported by Benjamin of Tudela. A clause in Sefer ha-Hillukim, 'the Easterners make Simhat Torah every year, the Palestinians every three and a half years', survives only in late recensions, and Shweka argues that it is not early evidence. How old Simhat Torah poetry is remains debated: Avraham Yaari (1964) is reported to have held that Palestinian piyyut has none, while Shulamit Elizur (2019) cites a Simhat Torah qedushta attributed to Kallir.
hedges: 'Jointly' is an inference by Fleischer and Shweka, supported by Benjamin of Tudela, not a statement of the manuscript.
Yaari's thesis is known here only through a secondary report.
Shlomo Naeh's proposal that the Palestinian cycle was designed to finish twice in seven years, at the Hakhel assembly of Sukkot, is a hypothesis (as cited by Shweka).

The colophon 'Simhat Torah was completed' (CUL Or. 1080 Box 3, fol. 54; 15 Av 1482 Sel. = 1171, as cited by Friedman) is not on the site; Friedman's 'Sunday' does not match the computed weekday (Monday).

contested.claim: Whether Palestinian piyyut had Simhat Torah poetry
positions: Yes: a qedushta attributed to Kallir (Elizur 2019, p. 834)

themes.title: Readings: haftarot, Targum and Psalms
themes.intro: Biblical books copied for synagogue use mark the festival readings in their rubrics rather than in their catalogue descriptions. Haftarot books carry decorated Aramaic headings such as 'דחג הסוכות' and 'דשמיני עצרת במלכים', and one gives the Simhat Torah haftarah from Joshua 1 with Targum Jonathan ('אפטרתא דיום שמחת תורה'). A psalter marks Psalm 122 in red as 'the psalm for the festival of Sukkot', and the Rylands exhibition catalogue From Cairo to Manchester identifies a leaf of Targum Onqelos as Leviticus 23:40-43, the Sukkot commandments. Of the 43 haftarot leaves found for the festival, 39 say nothing about Sukkot in their public description.
hedges: Rubrics are quoted from catalogue notes; the T-S B14.67 image may show another shelfmark and needs a human check before use.

themes.title: Sermons for the festival
themes.intro: Judaeo-Arabic sermons for the festival days survive in several collections. KTIV records homilies headed 'חג הסוכות אול יום' and 'חג הסוכות תאני יום' (Sukkot, first day; Sukkot, second day) on ENA 2708.14-15, and part of a homily for the second day of Sukkot on T-S NS 258.87; it titles Paris AIU IV.A.157 'a homily for Sukkot in Judaeo-Arabic', and the site's catalogue lists derashot for the second day of Sukkot on AIU IV.B.59. Whether these are copies of one work or simply the same genre has not been checked, and none has been identified with a known author.
hedges: Grouping these homilies as one work is a lead for a human check, not a finding.
The second-day heading on AIU IV.A.157 is visible only in machine text; its card uses the KTIV title alone.

themes.title: The law of the sukkah and the four species
themes.intro: The law of the festival is here in every layer the Genizah holds: Mishnah and Talmud tractate Sukkah, geonic responsa, the codes, Maimonides' Mishneh Torah and later commentaries. The most important single find is T-S F10.64, a leaf of Halakhot Gedolot whose margins carry excerpts of the Jerusalem Talmud, tractate Sukkah. Apart from the Leiden manuscript no other manuscript of Yerushalmi Sukkah survives, so these excerpts are a textual witness in their own right; they generally support the Venice glosses in Leiden (Sharlo, Ginzei Qedem 19, 2023; Sussmann's catalogue, no. 589). Rav Nissim Gaon's Judaeo-Arabic book on the laws of the lulav is identified by KTIV in Genizah fragments, following Shraga Abramson, and a Philadelphia fragment sets the laws of Sukkot in rhyme, in the strophic form of Ibn Gabirol's Azharot (Halper 258).
hedges: Abramson's page (Rav Nissim Gaon: Hamishah Sefarim, p. 165) has not been re-checked; do not attribute Or.1080 15.1 to Nissim Gaon on the page until it is.
Halper 258: the catalogue note says it cannot be ascertained whether the poem was ever part of synagogue liturgy.

themes.title: Later customs and Kabbalah
themes.intro: The Genizah kept receiving writings long after the classical period. Among its later Sukkot leaves are several that KTIV dates to the 16th-18th centuries: an order of the Ushpizin, the 'guests' welcomed into the sukkah each night, and kabbalistic intentions for waving the lulav and for the hakafot. Avraham Yaari's history of Simhat Torah (1964), as reported in a secondary source, dates the earliest record of hakafot on Simhat Torah to R. Isaac Tyrnau (14th-15th century) and credits the Safed practice of the Ari with spreading them.
hedges: Dates are KTIV's palaeographic ranges; Yaari is known here only through a secondary report.

themes.title: Fixing the festival: the calendar
themes.intro: The Palestinian leadership announced the year's calendar each year on the Mount of Olives during Sukkot; the Babylonian authorities did so a month earlier, at the Elul assembly (Stern 2019). Sukkot therefore marks a key moment in the calendar controversy of 921/2 between Saadya and Ben Meir. According to the Book of the Calendar Controversy, Ben Meir's son proclaimed in Jerusalem, on the 'Day of Assembly', that Marheshvan and Kislev would be defective; the passage survives on T-S NS 194.92 and ENA 2555.1. Which day that was is disputed (see below). Calendars also show how the festival was reckoned in daily life: the best-preserved booklet of Josiah b. Mevorakh al-ʿĀqūlī's 247-year calendar (T-S K2.8) has entries such as 'Sukkot and Shemini ʿAṣeret: Thursday; (day of the) Willow: Wednesday' (Vidro, 2017).
hedges: Gil is cited on both sides of the 921 question (Stern counts him for the second day; the Gil page in our corpus says Hoshana Rabbah), so do not assign him to either.
The 1296/7 date of the T-S K2.8 copy is from PGP/CUDL, not from the Fragment of the Month.

contested.claim: The day of the 921 proclamation ('Day of Assembly')
positions: Second day of Sukkot, 16 Tishri = Friday 21 September 921 ('probably'): Stern 2019, pp. 15, 121 n. 18, because the phrase is attested only for the Hakhel day
Hoshana Rabbah: Epstein, Malter, Bornstein and Fleischer; still Laufer 2025 ('27 September 921'; computed, Hoshana Rabbah 4682 fell on Wednesday 26 September 921)

themes.title: The assembly on the Mount of Olives
themes.intro: Each year at Sukkot the Palestinian yeshiva held its great assembly in Jerusalem. Laufer (2025), following Frenkel and Ben-Sasson, reconstructs it: a procession from the Priest's Gate up the Mount of Olives, the Gaon's sermon, appointments and titles, prayers for donors, excommunications (including a general ban on the Karaites) and the calendar proclamation. The best-documented crisis is Hoshana Rabbah 1029: Shelomo b. Yehuda reports that 'they ascended the Mount of Olives according to their custom', the ban on the Karaites and its aftermath (T-S Misc.35.11; Gil, doc. 85; Rustow 2008). In 1039 Natan b. Avraham urged his supporters to come to Jerusalem for the festival (T-S 10J9.25), and about 1045 a letter reports a sermon on the Mount 'on the day of ʿArava' and that only few pilgrims were present (T-S NS 320.42). The assembly ended when the yeshiva moved to Tyre in the 1070s, and Megillat Evyatar records assemblies re-staged at Tyre in 1081 and Haifa in 1082.
hedges: Rustow reads the Karaite ban as largely symbolic and treats Ibn Daud's picture of Karaites standing by at the ceremony as literary.

Laufer suggests that the ban on the Karaites was dropped after the Karaite Tustaris rose to power (after 1036); Or.1080 J45 (Gil's edition) reports a ban renewed on Shemini Atzeret 1038. Open question.
Freer F 43 (precedence settlement 'on the Day of Hoshanah [Rabbah] ... 4803'): Gottheil and Worrell give 8 October 1043; computed, 21 Tishri 4803 = Friday 8 October 1042.
The 'success' of the 1039 assembly is Gil's summary, not the letter's words.

themes.title: Palm branches, myrtle and citrons
themes.intro: Documents show the four species as a local economy. A lease of about 1150 on a date plantation belonging to the community's pious foundations obliges the tenant to 'cut one thousand palm branches ... and carry them to the Nile' (T-S 16.222; Gil, doc. 50); PGP infers that they were for Sukkot. Communal accounts of 1219 pay for carrying palm branches two days before the festival, and on the other side record Hoshana Rabbah expenses (T-S NS J221; Goitein, Med. Soc. II, App. B 48). The accounts of Shelomo b. Eliyyahu list 'myrtles [for the Sukkot Feast]' at 2 1/2 dirhams (T-S Misc.8.61), and letters order myrtle and 'beautiful and kosher' citrons, spelled turunj (תורנג) (T-S 8J27.12). The vocabulary is Judaeo-Arabic: turunj for citron, marsīn for myrtle, jarīd for palm fronds.
hedges: T-S 16.222: the Sukkot purpose of the palm branches is PGP's inference ('apparently').
T-S NS J221: PGP's 'Sept. 29, 1219' for the verso is wrong; 'Day of the Willow, Wednesday' computes to 2 October 1219 (Julian).

themes.title: The sukkah in the synagogue courtyard
themes.intro: S. D. Goitein observed that the miẓalla, the booth, is mentioned in Genizah documents 'thus far ... only in connection with the Jewish Feast of Tabernacles and only as situated in the court of a synagogue, not in that of a private home' (Med. Soc. IV, p. 77), and that the Genizah calls the festival 'Sukka' in the singular. The documents fit: the office of the Nagid Yehoshua (d. 1355) records an undertaking to build the booth of the Palestinians' synagogue (T-S K25.190), a pious-foundation account of 1165 pays for cleaning the channel behind that synagogue's sukkah (T-S Ar.18(1).155), and a letter to the Nagid Mevorakh laments the state of the sukkah of the Iraqis' synagogue (T-S 18J4.12).
hedges: Goitein elsewhere calls 'Sukka' as the festival's name 'typically Yemenite' (India Book II, 36, p. 396).
Khan's Arabic deed T-S Ar.38.117 puts a miẓalla in a house courtyard: an open question for Goitein's 'synagogue court only', not a refutation.

themes.title: Dated by the festival
themes.intro: Letters and deeds were often dated by the festival itself: 'on the eve of Sukkot', 'during the holiday', in the intermediate days or on the day after. A testimony written at Damietta in 1157 records that a man who had arrived on the eve of Sukkot with a charity letter from the Nagid sailed away 'on Sunday, the second day of Sukkot ... violating the holiday' (Bodl. MS heb. b 3/5, PGP; computed, 16 Tishri 4918 was indeed Sunday 22 September 1157). In Alexandria a letter reports great disturbances over bread 'on the second day of the Sukkot feast' (T-S 12.305), and in 1200 a writer in the intermediate days of the festival reports hunger and shortages (ENA NS 19.10). Contracts of 1543 and 1564 were written during the intermediate days (T-S 13J8.10; T-S NS J528).
hedges: T-S 13J8.10: PGP gives '= 1544 CE' for Tishri 5304; Sukkot 5304 fell in the autumn of 1543 (computed).
Computed dates are ours, in the Julian calendar before 1582.

themes.title: Letters, greetings and travellers
themes.intro: Merchants and scholars mention the festival in passing. From Qayrawan about 1020 the sons of Berakhya write to Ibn ʿAwkal that 'on this past Sukkot we would gather together and look into the matter of our Masters, the Heads of Yeshivot' (Yevr. III B 904). An Aden merchant of about 1130-50 had wanted to write 'in the days of Sukkot' (T-S 12.355; India Book II, no. 43). A Yom Kippur letter closes with blessings that include 'בירושלים ולראות סוכת דוד הנופ[לת] . . . השאובה' ('in Jerusalem, and to see the fallen booth of David ... the water-drawing'; ENA 2808.59, as excerpted by PGP).
hedges: ENA 2808.59: reading these closing blessings as Sukkot wishes is an interpretation of the PGP excerpt; the card quotes rather than asserts.

themes.title: Rabbanites and Karaites
themes.intro: Rabbanites and Karaites kept the festivals by different calendars, so the same festival could fall on different days, even within one household. The marriage contract of 1082 between the Rabbanite David b. Daniel and Nāshiya, from a Karaite family, has him undertake not to force her 'to profane her festivals [according to the Karaite calendar]', on condition that she observes the festivals according to the Rabbanite calendar with him (T-S 24.1). About 1030 a decree of the caliph al-Ẓāhir, answering a Rabbanite petition, ruled that neither group may interfere with the other, and that merchants of both may trade or abstain 'on their holidays' (T-S 13J7.29). The festival assembly on the Mount of Olives was also the occasion for bans on the Karaites (see the Mount of Olives theme).
hedges: T-S 24.1 and T-S 13J7.29 are not Sukkot-specific: the cards say 'festivals', not Sukkot.
The Karaite reading of Lev 23:40 with Neh 8:15 (the species as building material for the booth) is known from Karaite literature; no Genizah witness to it was verified.
RNL Evr. II A 145/16 and II A 2212 are late copies (1850s), not medieval witnesses.
